growth_story.headline: Steady but modest growth since the civil war ended; income per person hit a new high in 2025 as crime fell and remittances surged
growth_story.arc: Income per person shrank in most years from 1979 to 1989 during the civil war and did not get back to its 1978 level until 2012. Since 1990 the data show a single era: growth averaged 2.1 percent a year over 1990–2025, with no lasting shift of 2 points or more. The sources tell that era in phases: a strong post-peace start led by exports and private investment, a slower stretch after the 1995 Tequila crisis and full dollarization in 2001, and a modest pickup after 2010, with low investment and crime weighing on growth throughout. The pandemic cut income per person by 8.1 percent in 2020 before an 11.5 percent rebound in 2021. Growth averaged 2.3 percent a year over 2016–2025, up from 1.8 in the decade before, and a 3.5 percent rise in 2025 left income per person at its highest level yet. The World Bank and the IMF tie the recent pickup to a sharp fall in crime since 2022, record remittances and rising investment.

threads.title: War, collapse and peace
threads.text: Income per person fell in most years from 1979 to 1989 as civil war spread. Growth returned in the early 1990s after the 1992 peace accords, as reforms built an open, export-led economy.

threads.title: Slowdown and a dollar economy
threads.text: After the 1995 Tequila crisis, growth slowed through the late 1990s and the 2000s. The colón was pegged to the US dollar in 1993 and the economy became fully dollarized in 2001. The OECD links the slow years to low foreign and domestic investment and weak productivity growth.

threads.text: Money sent home by Salvadorans abroad pays for much of household spending on goods and local services. The World Bank says investment, exports and productivity have lagged behind, and the IMF warns that tighter immigration policies abroad could hit remittances and growth.

threads.title: Crime and the security turn
threads.text: For decades crime and violence raised costs for people and firms and cut the returns on investment. Since 2022 crime has fallen sharply, and the World Bank and the IMF credit this with lifting confidence and economic activity.

threads.text: The COVID-19 shock cut income per person by 8.1 percent in 2020. It bounced back by 11.5 percent in 2021, and growth then returned to its earlier pace.

since_last_year.text: Growth ran faster than the IMF expected. Income per person rose 3.5 percent in 2025, the fastest since 2006 apart from the 2021 rebound. The sources credit improved confidence, record remittances and buoyant investment. In October 2026 the IMF completed two more reviews of its lending program.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe a turn after crime fell in 2022, but income per person grew 2.6, 2.9 and 2.1 percent in 2022–2024, close to the decade average of 2.3; only 2025, at 3.5, stands clearly above it. The sources also tell the 1990s, 2000s and 2010s as distinct phases, while the data find one era since 1990 with no lasting shift of 2 points or more.
